symptoms were not alleviated after a follow-up period of 3 years. © 2007 movement disorder society key words: graves’ disease; stiff person syndrome; ataxia. stiff person syndrome (sps) is a rare central nervous system disorder, and is estimated to occur in /h110211 per million in the general population. 1 it is characterized by rigidity of the truncal and proximal limb muscles, epi- sodic spasms, and continuous motor unit activity even at rest. sps has been associated with other autoimmune diseases, such as type 1 diabetes mellitus and autoim- mune thyroid disease (hashimoto’s thyroiditis), among others. 2-8 however, while various movement disorders have been associated with hyperthyroidism, 9-12 the asso- ciation of sps with hyperthyroidism is extremely rare. we describe a patient with poorly uncontrolled graves’ disease and undiagnosed sps, who presented initially with acute ataxia simulating a cerebrovascular accident. case description a middle age chinese woman presented initially with signs and symptoms of hyperthyroidism and was subse- quently diagnosed to have graves’ disease. she was treated with carbimazole with little improvement of her thyroid condition. a few months later, she presented with the sud- den onset of slurred speech and rapidly progressing un- steady gait and was admitted for a probable cerebrovascular accident. she also complained of neck stiffness and back- ache about 2 weeks prior to her hospitalization . examina- tion revealed sinus tachycardia (heart rate 100/min), tem- perature of 37°c, and a small diffusely enlarged nontender goiter. she was alert and oriented, was noted to be dysar- thric, with bilateral rotatory and jerk nystagmus, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia and marked truncal ataxia. she had an increased extensor tone in her neck and trunk. no stimulus- induced or spontaneous bodily spasms were present . strength in her proximal muscles was slightly reduced, and the sensory examination was normal. her reﬂexes were not increased with bilateral ﬂexor plantar response. there was no ophthalmopathy or dermopathy. despite carbimazole treatment, her thyroid function tests revealed severe thyro- toxicosis (ft4 73.2 (9.6 –19.1 pmol/l), tsh /h110210.006 (0.36 –3.24 mu/l). her thyroid antibody proﬁle was con- sistent with graves’ disease [thyrototropin-binding inhibi- tory immunoglobulin (tbii) 28 (0 –1.5 u/l), thyroid per- oxidase antibody (tpoab) /h110223,000 (0 – 60 u/ml), thyroglobulin antibody (tgab) /h110222,000 (0 – 60 u/ml), thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin (tsi) /h110223,077 (50 – 179%)] (table 1). her father had type 2 diabetes mellitus but there was no family history of thyroid disease or multiple sclerosis. blood count, prothrombin and partial-thromboplastin times, liver and renal function tests, serum electrolytes, creatine kinase, and aldolase were normal. brain and cervical spine magnetic resonance imaging studies were unremarkable. magnetic resonance spectroscopic studies revealed a reduced myo-inositol and total choline in the frontal gray matter and parieto-occipital white matter. ct scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis, and mammo- gram revealed no abnormality. cerebrospinal ﬂuid (csf) examination was normal except for the presence of an oligoclonal band. electromyography of the axial muscles revealed continuous electrical discharges even in a re- laxed state. nerve conduction tests were normal. her glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody (gad ab) levels were grossly elevated [ /h11022187 (0 –9.5 u/l)]. an- tiamphiphysin antibody was not carried out . she was given a trial of plasmapheresis over 3 days, and subse- quently a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin therapy (ivig) at 0.4
